title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler recasts Lagrange's delta-calculus (1755/1760), which he had previously treated as a separate calculus, as part of the theory of functions of two variables (Institutiones calculi integralis, vol. III).

Top of page (end of §5/§6). All curves near the given curve y = X(x) can be written y = X + tV(x), with V arbitrary and t infinitely small. More generally, y may be any function y(x,t) of two variables, provided y(x,0) = X(x). This is the one-parameter embedding of the extremal candidate in a family of comparison curves.

First §7 (misnumbered; it should be §6). To form a variation, hold x fixed and differentiate only with respect to t. Take a first-kind expression Z(x,y) with dZ = M dx + N dy. Setting dx = 0 and dy = dt(∂y/∂t) gives the variation δZ = N dt(∂y/∂t), i.e. ∂Z/∂t = N ∂y/∂t. In modern terms this is the chain rule for the Gateaux derivative: δZ = Z_y δy, with δy = ∂y/∂t dt.

Second §7. Second-kind expressions also involve p = y_x, q = y_xx, r = y_xxx, and so on. Their variations are dt(∂p/∂t), dt(∂q/∂t), and so on. The next page then gives ∂p/∂t = ∂²y/∂x∂t etc., using the equality of mixed partials.

The point of the device is this: Lagrange had to postulate that δ and d commute (δdy = dδy). Here that becomes a consequence of the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives. This sets up §8 (δZ = N δy + P δp + Q δq + ...) and §9 (the variation of ∫Z dx, leading to the Euler–Lagrange equation by integration by parts).
errors: Section number 7 is printed twice in the original; the first '7.' should be '6.' This is a printing error, not a mathematical one.
Euler does not state that the variation is to be evaluated at t = 0. This is harmless to first order, but strictly δy = (∂y/∂t)|_{t=0} dt.

The claim that y = X + tV (or a general y(x,t)) 'comprehends all nearby curves' is heuristic. There is no specification of smoothness, of the function class, or of fixed endpoints. Equality of mixed partials is assumed without comment, which was standard for the time.

ideas.what: Embedding the unknown curve in a one-parameter family y(x,t) with y(x,0) = X, and defining the variation as the partial t-derivative
ideas.modern_name: One-parameter variation / Gateaux (first) variation, d/dt F[y + tη] at t = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E420, 1771/72), building on Lagrange's δ-method (1755/1762); the method's later standard form via Legendre, Jacobi, Weierstrass
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 16, 1772); foreshadowed in E385 (Inst. calc. int. III, appendix on calculus of variations); discussed by Goldstine, Fraser, Caratheodory's introduction to Opera omnia I.25

ideas.what: Variation of a point function Z(x,y): δZ = N δy with dx = 0
ideas.modern_name: Chain rule for the first variation

ideas.what: Variations of derivatives p, q, r are obtained as mixed partials ∂^{k+1}y/∂x^k∂t, so commutation of δ and d follows from symmetry of mixed partials
ideas.modern_name: Commutation of variation and differentiation, δ(y') = (δy)'
ideas.usually_credited_to: Postulated by Lagrange; derived this way by Euler 1771

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known foundational page of Euler's reformulation of the calculus of variations via an auxiliary parameter t. It is extensively discussed in histories of the subject (Goldstine, Fraser, Caratheodory's Opera omnia introduction), and nothing on it is unrecognized.
transcription_corrections: The page's two section headings both read '7.' in the original print; the first should logically be '6.' The transcription faithfully reproduces the printing error.
'vſurpari' and 'occurrant' are hyphenated across lines in the image ('vſur-pari', 'occur-rant'); the content is correct.
